one_liner: Go generic in-process cache implementing SIEVE and S3-FIFO eviction; about 16-18% fewer misses than hashicorp LRU, but no higher ops/sec.
what_it_does: A small Go generics library with two bounded in-memory caches, sieve.New[K,V](size, ttl) and s3fifo.New[K,V](size, ttl), behind one Cache interface (Set, Get, Peek, Contains, Remove, Len, Purge, Close, SetOnEvicted). It fills the same niche as hashicorp/golang-lru and groupcache/lru: a simple bounded cache where the eviction policy, not raw ops/sec, decides how many requests fall through to the backend. The API is close to hashicorp's but not identical: Set replaces Add (and returns nothing), an optional per-cache TTL runs a background sweeper goroutine, and the eviction callback reports why an entry left (evicted, expired or removed). Only SIEVE and S3-FIFO ship in this repo. TinyLFU, SLRU, S4LRU, Clock and 2Q in the README table are third-party libraries wired into the author's separate benchmark harness.
how_it_is_fast: The gain is fewer misses, not cheaper operations. SIEVE (NSDI'24) keeps one FIFO list plus a 'visited' bit per entry. A hit only sets the bit, and eviction walks a hand from the tail toward the head, clearing bits until it finds an unvisited entry. On Zipf-like traffic this keeps popular items and drops one-hit wonders quickly. S3-FIFO (SOSP'23) uses a small FIFO holding 10% of capacity, a main FIFO with a 2-bit frequency counter, and a ghost list of recently evicted keys, so one-hit wonders are filtered out before they reach the main queue. The README's claim that SIEVE hits need only a reader lock is out of date. v0.1.5 (January 2024) moved every call to an exclusive sync.Mutex after a data-race report (issue #21), so hits now serialize just as hashicorp's LRU Get does.
when_to_use: Go services with read-heavy, power-law (Zipf-like) key popularity, such as web or API response caching, where each miss costs a database or network round trip. In the author's harness SIEVE's hit rate beat hashicorp LRU's by about 11 points at a 0.1% cache and about 4 points at 10%.
Caches that are small relative to the key space (roughly 0.1-1% of distinct items), where the hit-ratio gap over LRU is widest.
Code already using hashicorp/golang-lru or groupcache/lru that wants a better eviction policy with little API churn and no runtime dependencies (standard library only).
Single-goroutine or low-contention callers. At concurrency=1 the harness had SIEVE at about 1.09x lru-hashicorp's QPS.
Cases needing one TTL for the whole cache plus an eviction callback that tells capacity evictions, expirations and explicit removals apart.
when_not_to_use: Throughput-bound, highly concurrent hot paths. Each cache uses one global mutex. In the author's harness SIEVE trailed both LRU baselines at 2-16 goroutines (0.66-0.87x lru-hashicorp QPS at 16 goroutines), golang-fifo's own S3-FIFO ran at about 0.6x, and otter and sharded freelru were much faster.
Scan-heavy or looping access patterns. The README says SIEVE is not scan-resistant; S3-FIFO or TinyLFU-style admission handles these better.
Workloads close to a 100% hit ratio. Both policies have O(n) worst-case eviction when every entry has been touched (issue #18, open since January 2024).

Large or GC-sensitive caches. Every entry is a heap object plus a container/list element holding a boxed key (the README appendix shows 4 allocs/op), and the README says the library does not try to compete with bigcache or freecache.
Cases needing Keys/Values iteration, Resize, GetOldest/RemoveOldest, per-entry TTL, cost- or byte-based sizing, or sharding. A sharded variant is still an open request (issue #24).

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (standard library container/list, sync, context, time); fortio.org/assert is used only by tests
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.24 (go.mod 'go 1.24'; CI tests on 1.24.x). The code needs generics and the Go 1.21 min builtin.
integration.platforms: any Go target (pure Go, no unsafe or assembly)
integration.thread_safety: Safe for concurrent use. Every SIEVE method, and every S3FIFO method except Len, takes one exclusive sync.Mutex, including Get. S3FIFO.Len reads its lists without the lock. A TTL > 0 starts one background goroutine per cache, which runs until Close is called.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the shape matches hashicorp/golang-lru v2 (generic K/V, Get/Peek/Contains/Remove/Len/Purge), but Add becomes Set with no evicted return, New returns no error (SIEVE panics if size <= 0), the callback gains an EvictReason argument, and Keys, Values, Resize, Cap, GetOldest, RemoveOldest, ContainsOrAdd and PeekOrAdd are missing. Unlike groupcache/lru it is generic and already locked.

gotchas: No published throughput number measures the shipping code. The README table (2023-12-12) and the harness tables (March 2024, pinned to golang-fifo v0.1.3) both come from before v0.1.5 replaced the RWMutex with a Mutex. The harness was bumped to v1.2.0 in July 2025, but its README results were not re-run. Hit rates depend only on the algorithm and should carry over; QPS should not be assumed to.

S3FIFO with TTL > 0 looks unsafe. Its addToBucket still computes the bucket index in int8 arithmetic, the same expression PR #32 fixed in SIEVE after an 'index out of range [-28]' panic, and no S3FIFO test calls Set after the cleanup counter passes 28. S3FIFO.New also skips SIEVE's size check, and S3FIFO.Purge leaves TTL bucket entries behind.

Expiry is enforced only by the background sweeper, which cycles through 100 time buckets and ticks every ttl/100. Get does not check an entry's expiry time, so an expired value can be returned until its bucket is swept. TTL caches that are never Closed leak their sweeper goroutine.

The eviction callback runs while the cache mutex is held, so calling the same cache from inside it will deadlock (sync.Mutex is not reentrant). SIEVE's Close/Purge fires the callback with EvictReasonRemoved for every remaining entry, while S3FIFO's Purge fires none.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued SIEVE and S3-FIFO entries are libCacheSim simulators and CacheLib prototypes, and Caffeine and W-TinyLFU target the JVM and C++. Pick this one when you need those eviction policies as an importable Go package with an LRU-like API. If your Go hot path is limited by lock contention rather than misses, the author's own harness points to otter or sharded freelru (not catalogued) instead.
verified_claims_summary: The author's go-cache-benchmark harness runs a Get-then-Set-on-miss loop over 7.5M Zipf(0.99) string keys drawn from 500K items. Results are single runs on an unnamed desktop, with go.mod at Go 1.22 and golang-fifo v0.1.3. They show SIEVE with 16-18% fewer misses than hashicorp/golang-lru v2 at 0.1%, 1% and 10% cache sizes, but lower QPS at 2-16 goroutines (for example 2.64M vs 3.05M ops/s at 16 goroutines with a 0.1% cache) and higher QPS only single-threaded (5.05M vs 4.65M). The README's headline 2.51M vs 2.06M QPS row comes from an older (2023-12-12) run of the same harness, which the later tables contradict. No CPU model, compiler flags or repeat runs are reported for any of these comparisons.
status_note: Stale: the last release, v1.2.0 on 2025-05-10, only bumped Go to 1.24, and sharding (#24), O(n) worst-case eviction (#18) and concurrency tests (#22) remain open. Still, it is MIT-licensed, about 700 lines with no runtime dependencies and easy to vendor, and pkg.go.dev lists a handful of importers, including redpanda-operator.
